claim: Recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV) has been widely used as a viral vector across mammalian biology.
source: Recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV) has been widely used as a viral vector across mammalian biology and has been shown to be safe and effective in human gene therapy.
evidence: This is a general statement about the widespread use of rAAV in the field, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: rAAV has been shown to be safe and effective in human gene therapy.
source: Recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV) has been widely used as a viral vector across mammalian biology and has been shown to be safe and effective in human gene therapy.
evidence: This statement references the established safety and efficacy profile of rAAV in gene therapy applications.

claim: Neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and immature dentate granule cells (DGCs) within the adult murine hippocampus are particularly sensitive to rAAV-induced cell death.
source: We demonstrate that neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and immature dentate granule cells (DGCs) within the adult murine hippocampus are particularly sensitive to rAAV-induced cell death.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: rAAV-induced cell loss is dose dependent.
source: Cell loss is dose dependent and nearly complete at experimentally relevant viral titers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D demonstrating varying levels of cell loss at different viral titers.

claim: rAAV-induced cell loss is nearly complete at experimentally relevant viral titers.
source: Cell loss is dose dependent and nearly complete at experimentally relevant viral titers.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data showing >80% loss of BrdU+ cells at 3e12 gc/mL titer (Figure 1D).

claim: rAAV-induced cell death is rapid, with loss of BrdU-labeled cells within 18 hr post-injection.
source: rAAV-induced cell death is rapid and persistent, with loss of BrdU-labeled cells within 18 hr post-injection and no evidence of recovery of adult neurogenesis at 3 months post-injection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2J showing significant BrdU+ cell loss at 18 hours.

claim: There is no evidence of recovery of adult neurogenesis at 3 months post-injection of rAAV.
source: rAAV-induced cell death is rapid and persistent, with loss of BrdU-labeled cells within 18 hr post-injection and no evidence of recovery of adult neurogenesis at 3 months post-injection.
evidence: This is supported by DCX intensity measurements at 3 months showing persistent loss (Figure 2G).

claim: The remaining mature DGCs appear hyperactive 4 weeks post-injection based on immediate early gene expression.
source: The remaining mature DGCs appear hyperactive 4 weeks post-injection based on immediate early gene expression, consistent with previous studies investigating the effects of attenuating adult neurogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by cFOS expression data in Figure 4A,B showing increased activation in mature DGCs.

claim: In vitro application of AAV is sufficient to induce cell death.
source: In vitro application of AAV or electroporation of AAV2 inverted terminal repeats (ITRs) is sufficient to induce cell death.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experiments shown in Figure 3A-C demonstrating dose-dependent cell death.

claim: Electroporation of AAV2 inverted terminal repeats (ITRs) is sufficient to induce cell death.
source: In vitro application of AAV or electroporation of AAV2 inverted terminal repeats (ITRs) is sufficient to induce cell death.
evidence: This is supported by electroporation experiments in Figure 3D-H showing ITR-induced toxicity.

claim: Efficient transduction of the dentate gyrus (DG) without ablating adult neurogenesis can be achieved by injection of rAAV2-retro serotyped virus into CA3.
source: Efficient transduction of the dentategyrus (DG)– without ablating adult neurogenesis– can be achieved by injection of rAAV2-retro serotyped virus into CA3.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4D-F showing preserved neurogenesis markers with AAV retro.

claim: rAAV2-retro results in efficient retrograde labeling of mature DGCs.
source: rAAV2-retro results in efficient retrograde labeling of mature DGCs and permits in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of dentate activity while leaving adult neurogenesis intact.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 4G-L showing labeled DGCs with calcium activity.

claim: rAAV2-retro permits in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of dentate activity while leaving adult neurogenesis intact.
source: rAAV2-retro results in efficient retrograde labeling of mature DGCs and permits in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of dentate activity while leaving adult neurogenesis intact.
evidence: This is supported by combined imaging and histology data in Figure 4 showing functional imaging with preserved neurogenesis.

claim: The subgranular zone (SGZ) of the hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) is one of only a few regions of the mammalian brain that continues to exhibit neurogenesis into adulthood.
source: The subgranular zone (SGZ) of the hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) is one of only a few regions of the mammalian brain that continues to exhibit neurogenesis into adulthood.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about adult neurogenesis in the mammalian brain.

claim: Adult-born dentate granule cells (abDGCs) are continuously generated from a pool of largely quiescent neural stem cells.
source: Adult-born dentate granule cells (abDGCs) are continuously generated from a pool of largely quiescent neural stem cells that undergo proliferation, differentiation, and fate specification before maturing into neurons that are indistinguishable from developmentally derived dentate granule cells (DGCs) (Gonçalves et al., 2016; Kempermann et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on adult neurogenesis.

claim: Neural stem cells and their immature progeny are sensitive to environmental stimuli.
source: These stem cells and their immature progeny are sensitive to environmental stimuli; their proliferation, development, and survival are regulated by multiple intrinsic and extrinsic factors, including experience, stress, inflammation, and pharmacologic agents (see Materials and methods, Gonçalves et al., 2016; Kempermann et al., 2015; Monje et al., 2003; Snyder et al., 2009; Vivar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research on factors affecting neurogenesis.

claim: abDGCs are critical for maintaining the physiological activity of mature DGCs.
source: Numerous studies demonstrate that abDGCs are critical for maintaining the physiological activity of mature DGCs and contribute to hippocampus-dependent behaviors (Clelland et al., 2009; Deng et al., 2009; Deng et al., 2010; Ikrar et al., 2013; Lacefield et al., 2012; Nakashiba et al., 2012; Sahay et al., 2011; Saxe et al., 2007; Tronel et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: abDGCs contribute to hippocampus-dependent behaviors.
source: Numerous studies demonstrate that abDGCs are critical for maintaining the physiological activity of mature DGCs and contribute to hippocampus-dependent behaviors (Clelland et al., 2009; Deng et al., 2009; Deng et al., 2010; Ikrar et al., 2013; Lacefield et al., 2012; Nakashiba et al., 2012; Sahay et al., 2011; Saxe et al., 2007; Tronel et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Wild-type AAV is a non-enveloped, single-stranded DNA virus endemic to humans and primates.
source: Wild-type AAV is a non-enveloped, single-stranded DNA virus endemic to humans and primates and has been previously proposed to have no known pathogenicity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the characteristics of wild-type AAV.

claim: Wild-type AAV has been previously proposed to have no known pathogenicity.
source: Wild-type AAV is a non-enveloped, single-stranded DNA virus endemic to humans and primates and has been previously proposed to have no known pathogenicity.
evidence: This references the historical understanding of AAV safety.

claim: Wild-type AAV contains a 4.7 kb genome that includes the Rep and Cap genes and a pair of palindromic 145 bp inverted terminal repeats (ITRs).
source: This replication-defective virus contains a 4.7 kb genome that includes the Rep and Cap genes and a pair of palindromic 145 bp inverted terminal repeats (ITRs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of the AAV genome.

claim: rAAV retains only the ITRs from the original wild-type genome.
source: The Rep and Cap genes can be supplied in trans to create space for incorporating transgenes of interest, yielding the widely used rAAV, which retains only the ITRs from the original wild-type genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of recombinant AAV vectors.

claim: rAAV is often used to deliver a variety of genetically encoded tools to specific cell types and brain regions.
source: In experimental neuroscience, rAAV is often used to deliver a variety of genetically encoded tools, including actuators and sensors of neuronal function, to specific cell types and brain regions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the use of rAAV in neuroscience research.

claim: rAAV's minimal viral genome and limited immunogenicity and toxicity have made it the vector of choice for human gene therapy.
source: In addition, rAAV's minimal viral genome and limited immunogenicity and toxicity have made it the vector of choice for human gene therapy (Büning and Schmidt, 2015; Choudhury et al., 2017; Hocquemiller et al., 2016; Hudry and Vandenberghe, 2019), including two FDA-approved therapies for disorders of the CNS (Hoy, 2019; Smalley, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews on AAV gene therapy and references to FDA approvals.

claim: There are two FDA-approved therapies using rAAV for disorders of the CNS.
source: In addition, rAAV's minimal viral genome and limited immunogenicity and toxicity have made it the vector of choice for human gene therapy (Büning and Schmidt, 2015; Choudhury et al., 2017; Hocquemiller et al., 2016; Hudry and Vandenberghe, 2019), including two FDA-approved therapies for disorders of the CNS (Hoy, 2019; Smalley, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to publications about FDA-approved AAV therapies.

claim: rAAV has increasingly been reported to demonstrate toxicity in some cell types.
source: Despite its safety profile, rAAV has increasingly been reported to demonstrate toxicity in some cell types (Bockstael et al., 2012; Hinderer et al., 2018; Hirsch et al., 2011; Hordeaux et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous reports of AAV toxicity.

claim: The toxic effects of rAAV on abDGCs have previously not been assessed.
source: However, the toxic effects of rAAV on abDGCs have previously not been assessed.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Delivery of calcium indicators via commonly used rAAV serotypes resulted in a dramatic qualitative loss of the immature neuron marker doublecortin (DCX) 2 weeks after viral injection.
source: In preliminary studies, we found that the delivery of calcium indicators via commonly used rAAV serotypes at doses equivalent to or below previously reported doses resulted in a dramatic qualitative loss of the immature neuron marker doublecortin (DCX) 2 weeks after viral injection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qualitative observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The effect of rAAV on DCX occurred following the injection of a variety of rAAV preparations, regardless of vector production facility, purification method, capsid serotype, promoter, and protein expression.
source: This effect occurred following the injection of a variety of rAAV preparations, regardless of vector production facility (Salk Institute Viral Vector Core, University of Pennsylvania Vector Core, Addgene), purification method (iodixanol, CsCl), capsid serotype (AAV1 and AAV8; all incorporating AAV2 ITRs), promoter (CAG, Syn, CaMKIIa), and protein expression (GFP, jRGECO1a, a red calcium indicator, and mCherry) at doses typically required for the functional manipulation or visualization of DGCs in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by data from multiple viral preparations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cells that were 2 days old and younger at the time of rAAV injection were almost completely eliminated within 48 hr.
source: Cells that were 2 days old and younger at the time of injection were almost completely eliminated within 48 hr (−83.9 ± 6.7%, p<0.001, all textual results reported as change relative to the mean of non-injected contralateral DG ± standard error of the mean difference, unless stated otherwise).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from BrdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cells that were 7–9 days old at the time of rAAV injection were partially protected.
source: Cells that were 7–9 days old were partially protected (−41.3 ± 6.3%, p<0.001), whereas cells that were 14–16 days old were largely protected with variable but non-significant loss (−15.4 ± 6.3%, n.s.).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from BrdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cells that were 14–16 days old at the time of rAAV injection were largely protected with variable but non-significant loss.
source: Cells that were 7–9 days old were partially protected (−41.3 ± 6.3%, p<0.001), whereas cells that were 14–16 days old were largely protected with variable but non-significant loss (−15.4 ± 6.3%, n.s.).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from BrdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Fully mature abDGCs, approximately 8 weeks old, did not demonstrate significant loss at 1 week following AAV injection.
source: Fully mature abDGCs, approximately 8 weeks old (Laplagne et al., 2007; Piatti et al., 2013), also did not demonstrate significant loss at 1 week following AAV injection (−4.5 ± 6.3%, n.s.; Figure 1B last column).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from BrdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 1B, with citations supporting the age definition.

claim: Tbr2+ intermediate progenitors were lost even when mature BrdU+ cells were spared.
source: In the same tissue, Tbr2+ intermediate progenitors were lost even when mature BrdU+ cells were spared, demonstrating that the virus did not lack toxicity in these animals (Ftreatment x time(3,27)=3.0, p<0.05; 0 weeks: −80.2 ± 9.1%, p<0.001; 1 weeks: −76.9 ± 8.5%, p<0.001; 2 weeks: −82.6 ± 8.5%, p<0.001; 8 weeks: −50.8 ± 8.5%, p<0.001; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Injection of empty AAV viral capsid containing no viral DNA into the DG had no effect on BrdU+ cells at 1 week post-injection.
source: At 1 week post-injection, there was no effect on BrdU+ cells (2 days old at the time of empty capsid injection) relative to the contralateral control DG, although there was a mild decrease 4 weeks post-injection that did not recapitulate the severe loss observed with intact virus (Ftreatment x time(1,14)=6.5, p<0.05, 1 week post-injection: 6.2 ± 5.7%, n.s., Figure 1B, first column; 4 weeks: −14.5 ± 5.7%, p<0.05, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A near complete ablation of BrdU+ cells was seen in the DG injected with 1 µL 3 E12 GC/mL rAAV.
source: A nearly complete ablation of BrdU+ cells was seen in the DG injected with 3 e12 gc/mL rAAV (−84.3 ± 6.7%, p<0.001), whereas partial ablation of BrdU+ cells resulted from the injection of 1 e12 gc/mL rAAV (−52.1 ± 6.7%, p<0.001), and a small but significant reduction of adult neurogenesis resulted from injection of 3e11 gc/mL rAAV (−23.4 ± 7.2%, p<0.01; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D demonstrating dose-dependent effects.

claim: Partial ablation of BrdU+ cells resulted from the injection of 1 e12 gc/mL rAAV.
source: A nearly complete ablation of BrdU+ cells was seen in the DG injected with 3 e12 gc/mL rAAV (−84.3 ± 6.7%, p<0.001), whereas partial ablation of BrdU+ cells resulted from the injection of 1 e12 gc/mL rAAV (−52.1 ± 6.7%, p<0.001), and a small but significant reduction of adult neurogenesis resulted from injection of 3e11 gc/mL rAAV (−23.4 ± 7.2%, p<0.01; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D demonstrating dose-dependent effects.

claim: A small but significant reduction of adult neurogenesis resulted from injection of 3e11 gc/mL rAAV.
source: A nearly complete ablation of BrdU+ cells was seen in the DG injected with 3 e12 gc/mL rAAV (−84.3 ± 6.7%, p<0.001), whereas partial ablation of BrdU+ cells resulted from the injection of 1 e12 gc/mL rAAV (−52.1 ± 6.7%, p<0.001), and a small but significant reduction of adult neurogenesis resulted from injection of 3e11 gc/mL rAAV (−23.4 ± 7.2%, p<0.01; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D demonstrating dose-dependent effects.

claim: The number of Sox2+ cells within the SGZ was modestly decreased following rAAV injection.
source: The number of Sox2+ cells within the SGZ was modestly decreased (Ftreatment(1,19)=15.5, p<0.001; Ftime(2,19)=1.6, n.s.; Ftreatment x time(2,19)=2.7, n.s.; Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Tbr2+ intermediate progenitor cells were almost entirely lost and did not show signs of recovery by 4 weeks post-injection.
source: In contrast, Tbr2+ intermediate progenitor cells were almost entirely lost and did not show signs of recovery by 4 weeks post-injection (Ftreatment(1,19)=129.2, p<0.001; Ftime(2,19)=0.1, n.s.; Ftreatment x time(2,19)=0.2, n.s.; Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B,D.

claim: Expression of DCX showed progressive decline until near complete loss at 4 weeks post-injection.
source: Expression of the late premitotic and immature neuronal marker DCX showed progressive decline until near complete loss at 4 weeks post-injection (Ftreatment x time(3,27)=12.8, p<0.001; 2 days: −27.7 ± 7.5%, p<0.01; 1 week: −58.7 ± 7.0%, p<0.001; 4 weeks: −92.0 ± 7.5%, p<0.001; Figure 2B,G) and did not show signs of recovery 3 months post-injection (−68.7 ± 6.6%, p<0.001; Figure 2G, last column).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B,G.

claim: DCX expression did not show signs of recovery 3 months post-injection.
source: Expression of the late premitotic and immature neuronal marker DCX showed progressive decline until near complete loss at 4 weeks post-injection (Ftreatment x time(3,27)=12.8, p<0.001; 2 days: −27.7 ± 7.5%, p<0.01; 1 week: −58.7 ± 7.0%, p<0.001; 4 weeks: −92.0 ± 7.5%, p<0.001; Figure 2B,G) and did not show signs of recovery 3 months post-injection (−68.7 ± 6.6%, p<0.001; Figure 2G, last column).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Injection of empty AAV viral capsid alone did not result in a reduction of Tbr2+ or DCX+ cells at 1 or 4 weeks post-injection.
source: Injection of empty AAV viral capsid (Figure 2E) alone did not result in a reduction of Tbr2+ or DCX+ cells at 1 or 4 weeks post-injection (Tbr2: Ftreatment(1,10)=6.4e-5, n.s. Ftime(1,10)=0.3, n.s.; Ftreatment x time(1,10)=1.8, n.s; Figure 2F; DCX: Ftreatment(1,14)=3.9, n.s.; Ftime(1,14)=0.7, n.s.; Ftreatment x time(1,14)=1.3, n.s.; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Viral DNA is required for rAAV-induced cell loss.
source: These results demonstrate that viral DNA is required for cell loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between intact virus and empty capsid experiments.

claim: A majority of Sox2+ cells remaining 1 week after rAAV infection are GFP positive.
source: A majority of Sox2+ cells remaining 1 week after rAAV infection are GFP positive, indicating that these cells survive despite the vast majority being infected by rAAV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,F; 75.6 ± 11.5%).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative colocalization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,F.

claim: Only a minority of surviving DCX+ cells expressed GFP 1 week after rAAV infection.
source: However, only a minority of surviving DCX+ cells expressed GFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,F; 35.9 ± 12.3%), and of the few remaining Tbr2 cells, few expressed GFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F; 7.1 ± 10.7%​), suggesting a survivorship bias for cells not infected by rAAV when examining populations with substantial loss.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative colocalization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,F.

claim: Variation in viral tropism is not likely to explain the measurable differences in AAV toxicity across cell types.
source: Overall, we observed an increasing percentage of GFP-expressing cells with increasing survival across the three populations, suggesting that variation in viral tropism is not likely to explain the measurable differences in AAV toxicity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of GFP colocalization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Nearly all of the BrdU+-dividing cells gained from enrichment and exercise were eliminated by rAAV.
source: Nearly all of the BrdU+-dividing cells gained from enrichment and exercise were eliminated by rAAV (Fhousing(1,14)=8.7, p<0.01; Ftreatment(1,14)=124.0, p<0.001; Fhousing x treatment (1,14)=9.4, p<0.01; home cage: −79.5 ± 13.9%, p<0.001; enriched environment: −139.9 ± 13.9%, p<0.001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from enriched environment experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Environmental enrichment is insufficient to prevent rAAV-induced cell loss.
source: These results indicate that proliferating cells are the primary target of the virus and that environmental enrichment is insufficient to prevent cell loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the enriched environment experiments showing continued cell loss despite increased neurogenesis.

claim: rAAV-injected DGs showed a modest decrease in BrdU+ cells at 12 and 18 hr relative to their contralateral saline-injected control.
source: rAAV-injected DGs already showed a modest decrease in BrdU+ cells at 12 and 18 hr relative to their contralateral saline-injected control (Ftreatment(1,13)=13.9, p<0.01; Ftime(1,13)=0.04, n.s.; Ftreatment x time(1,13)=0.07, n.s.; Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from acute time-course experiments shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The same decrease in Tbr2+ cells was seen at 12 and 18 hr following rAAV injection.
source: The same decrease was seen in Tbr2+ cells (Ftreatment(1,13)=16.5, p<0.001.; Ftime(1,13)=0.4, n.s.; Ftreatment x time(1,13)=3.3, n.s.; Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from acute time-course experiments shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Cell loss was accompanied by an increased number of Caspase-3+ apoptotic cells relative to saline-injected controls at 12 hr.
source: Cell loss was accompanied by an increased number of Caspase-3+ apoptotic cells relative to saline-injected controls at 12 hr (Ftreatment x time(1,13)=21.2, p<0.001; 12 hr treatment: +188.6 ± 29.8%, p <0.001; 18 hr treatment: 11.7 ± 24.3%, n.s.; Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from acute time-course experiments shown in Figure 2L.

claim: A significant increase in pyknosis was seen in BrdU+ proliferating cells at 12 hr following rAAV injection.
source: Although the increase in total pyknotic and karyorrhexic cells in rAAV-injected DG was short of significant (p=0.058), (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K), a significant increase in pyknosis was seen in BrdU+ proliferating cells (2.3 ± 0.7 additional cells/section, p<0.05; Figure 2M).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from acute time-course experiments shown in Figure 2M.

claim: rAAV increases programmed cell death of dividing and recently divided cells in the DG.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that rAAV increases programmed cell death of dividing and recently divided cells in the DG.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on caspase-3 activation and pyknosis in BrdU+ cells.

claim: Rapid (<48 hr) loss of NPCs occurred independent of expression of the microglial marker Iba1.
source: However, rapid (<48 hr) loss of NPCs (Figure 2) occurred independent of expression of the microglial marker Iba1, which did not increase until 4 weeks post-injection (Ftreatment x time(2,19)=54.6, p<0.001; 2 days:18.6 ± 10.3%, n.s.; 1 week: −9.0 ± 9.7%, n.s.; 4 weeks: 132.4 ± 10.34%, p<0.001; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data on Iba1 expression shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Expression of the astrocyte marker GFAP was unchanged in the SGZ and hilus at 2 days post-injection.
source: Similarly, expression of the astrocyte marker GFAP was unchanged in the SGZ and hilus at 2 days post-injection, slightly increased at 1 week, and greatly increased at 4 weeks (Ftreatment x time(2,19)=91.0, p<0.001; 2 days: 21.6 ± 8.7%, n.s.; 1 week: 25.2 ± 8.1%, p<0.05; 4 weeks: 165.5 ± 8.7%, p<0.001; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data on GFAP expression shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: AAV-induced toxicity may be cell autonomous.
source: These findings suggest that AAV-induced toxicity may be cell autonomous and is unlikely to be mediated by astrocyte- or microglia-activated immune responses or by inflammatory signals and other indirect or local changes within the niche.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of cell loss relative to inflammation and from small volume injection experiments.

claim: rAAV-induced toxicity was not altered in Sting knockout mice.
source: Additionally, we found that rAAV-induced toxicity was not altered in Sting knockout mice and, therefore, likely not dependent on foreign nucleic acid detection through Sting-mediated pathways (BrdU: −90.2% ± 14.2, p<0.001; Tbr2: −88.7 ± 12.9%, p<0.001; Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from Sting-KO experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Dose-dependent inhibition of NPC proliferation was most profound in NPCs infected with rAAV 1 e7 MOI.
source: Dose-dependent inhibition of NPC proliferation and cell death was most profound in NPCs infected with rAAV 1 e7 MOI and moderate in NPCs infected with 1 e6 MOI.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: Within 24 hr of rAAV application at 1 e7 MOI, NPCs had ceased to proliferate.
source: Within 24 hr of rAAV application, NPCs infected with 1 e7 MOI had ceased to proliferate, whereas application of 1 e6 MOI resulted in comparatively slower proliferation compared to PBS control.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: NPCs infected with 1 e7 MOI showed the most significant increase in cell death.
source: Cell death, visualized by permeability to propidium iodide, also showed a dose-dependent increase. NPCs infected with 1 e7 MOI showed the most significant increase in cell death, whereas NPCs infected with 1 e6 MOI showed an intermediate increase.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Electroporation of 5 e6 ITR is sufficient to result in cell loss within hours of electroporation and arrest of proliferation by 40 hr.
source: In the high-dose ITR condition, NPCs were significantly decreased by 6 hr post-electroporation (Ftreatment(4,200)=630.2, p<0.001; Ftime(19,200)=635.0, p<0.001; Ftreatment x time(76,200)=6.0, p<0.001; 6 hr ITR 5 e6 vs PBS: −8.1% ± 2.5, p<0.05) and had ceased expansion by 40 hr (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro electroporation imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The proportion of cells in S/G2 phase that were dying was greatly increased at 12 and 24 hr in the high ITR condition.
source: FACS analysis at 12, 24, and 36 hr showed the proportion of cells in S/G2 phase that were dying (UVZombie+) was greatly increased at 12 and 24 hr in the high ITR condition, but not in the other experimental groups relative to PBS control (Ftreatment(4,30)=9.5, p<0.001; Ftime(2,30)=23.3, p<0.001; Ftreatment x time(8,30)=2.2, p<0.05; 12 hr ITR 5e6 vs PBS +12.0 ± 2.0%, p<0.001, Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Mature DGC cFOS activation showed an inverse relationship with the level of adult neurogenesis.
source: Consistent with previous studies examining the effects of manipulating adult neurogenesis on DG activity (Ikrar et al., 2013), mature DGC cFOS activation showed an inverse relationship with the level of adult neurogenesis (Ftreatment x time(2,20) = 11.4, p<0.001; Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4A,B and citations to previous studies.

claim: Injection with 1 µL 3 e12 gc/mL rAAV resulted in the largest increase in mature DGC cFOS activation.
source: Injection with 1 µL 3 e12 gc/mL rAAV, which ablates over 80% of BrdU+ cells (Figure 1D), resulted in the largest increase in mature DGC cFOS activation (81.6±13.6 additional cells per section, p<0.001); 1 µL 1 e12 gc/mL rAAV injection resulted in a moderate and more variable increase (40.0 ± 13.6 additional cells per section, p<0.05), and 1 µL 3 e11 gc/mL rAAV injection demonstrated no significant change on average (-13.3 ± 14.5 additional cells per section, n.s.).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: cFOS activation and loss of BrdU+ cells were significantly correlated.
source: cFOS activation and loss of BrdU+ cells were significantly correlated (slope = 0.26, R2=0.59, p<0.001; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Adult neurogenesis was intact 2 weeks after AAV retro injection relative to the uninjected contralateral hippocampus.
source: Histology performed following two-photon calcium imaging confirmed that adult neurogenesis was intact 2 weeks after injection relative to the uninjected contralateral hippocampus (Tbr2: +4.7 ± 7.0%, t(5)=0.7, n.s. Figure 4D,E; DCX +14.3 ± 6.3%, t(5)=4.3, p<0.01, Figure 4D,F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative histology data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: A similar number of DGCs was identified across animals using AAV retro.
source: A similar number of DGCs was identified across animals (255.3 ± 20.5 cells/DG; Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Total activity of DGCs was demonstrated to be sparse.
source: Total activity of these cells was demonstrated to be sparse (282.9 ±104.5 events/minute; Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Approximately one quarter of DGCs were active in any given minute during imaging.
source: Approximately one quarter of the cells were active in any given minute during imaging (24.3 ± 7.6% cells active/minute; Figure 4K), with a small number of calcium transients per active cell observed per minute (2.0 ± 0.4 events/active cell/minute; Figure 4L).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The limited activity of DGCs measured with AAV retro is consistent with previous imaging studies in the DG.
source: The limited activity of DGCs measured in our study with AAV retro is consistent with previous imaging studies in the DG (Danielson et al., 2016; Pilz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited previous studies.

claim: The doses demonstrated to ablate neurogenesis are within or below the range of experimentally relevant titers commonly injected into the mouse DG.
source: The doses demonstrated to ablate neurogenesis are within or below the range of experimentally relevant titers commonly injected into the mouse DG, 1.5 e12 to 3.6 e13 gc/mL (Anacker et al., 2018; Castle et al., 2018; Danielson et al., 2016; Danielson et al., 2017; Gong and Zhou, 2018; Hashimotodani et al., 2017; Hayashi et al., 2017; Kaspar et al., 2002; Kirschen et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2012; McAvoy et al., 2016; Ni et al., 2019; Pilz et al., 2016; Ramirez et al., 2015; Raza et al., 2017; Redondo et al., 2014; Senzai and Buzsáki, 2017; Swiech et al., 2015; Zetsche et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies using similar viral titers.

claim: rAAV-induced cell death appears to be cell autonomous and mediated by AAV2 ITRs.
source: This process appears to be cell autonomous and mediated by AAV2 ITRs, which are used nearly universally in rAAVs.
evidence: This is inferred from in vitro experiments showing ITR-induced toxicity and spatial restriction of toxicity in vivo.

claim: Elimination of 4-week-old abDGCs by rAAV alters the activity of mature DGCs, resulting in DG hyperactivity.
source: Consistent with previous ablation studies, elimination of 4-week-old abDGCs by rAAV alters the activity of mature DGCs, resulting in DG hyperactivity (as indicated by cFOS expression).
evidence: This is supported by cFOS expression data in Figure 4A,B and citations to previous ablation studies.

claim: The Tbr2+ population replenishes DCX+ progenitors and immature neurons under physiological conditions.
source: Under physiological conditions, the Tbr2+ population replenishes DCX+ progenitors and immature neurons, which can retain expression of the DCX protein in the mouse for more than 3 weeks post-mitosis (Kempermann et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about neurogenesis supported by a citation.

claim: The total number of Sox2+ cells, composed of Type 1 and 2a NPCs, was relatively unaffected by rAAV.
source: Interestingly, the total number of Sox2+ cells, composed of Type 1 and 2a NPCs, was relatively unaffected by rAAV, consistent with this population being largely quiescent (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Administration of high-dose ITR oligonucleotides resulted in a disproportionate loss of dividing cells.
source: Analysis with FACS demonstrated that administration of high-dose ITR oligonucleotides resulted in a disproportionate loss of dividing cells (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: A developmental window exists where actively dividing Type 2 NPCs and recently post-mitotic immature neurons are sensitive to rAAV-induced cell death.
source: To a large extent, this finding seems to recapitulate in vivo experiments, which demonstrate that a developmental window exists where actively dividing Type 2 NPCs and recently post-mitotic immature neurons are sensitive to rAAV-induced cell death, whereas rarely dividing neural stem cells and mature abDGCs flanking this window are significantly less affected.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined in vitro and in vivo experimental data.

claim: Infections involving cytomegalovirus, rubella, varicella-zoster, herpes simplex, HIV, and Zika have been implicated in the pathogenesis of microcephaly.
source: Infections involving a number of viruses, including cytomegalovirus (CMV), rubella, varicella-zoster, herpes simplex, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and Zika, have been implicated in the pathogenesis of microcephaly, the abnormal development of the cerebral cortex resulting in small head size.
evidence: This is established knowledge about viral causes of microcephaly.

claim: There is evidence that these viruses cause microcephaly through the elimination of NPC populations.
source: There is evidence that these viruses cause microcephaly through the elimination of NPC populations (Devakumar et al., 2018) in HIV (Balinang et al., 2017; Schwartz et al., 2007), CMV (Luo et al., 2010; Teissier et al., 2014), and Zika virus (Garcez et al., 2016; Qian et al., 2016) among others.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on viral effects on NPCs.

claim: Zika virus attenuates proliferation and neurogenesis in the adult mouse DG.
source: Perhaps the best studied among these is Zika virus, which, similar to rAAV, attenuates proliferation and neurogenesis in the adult mouse DG, demonstrating a marked loss of EdU+ cells following infection (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research on Zika virus effects.

claim: rAAV offers a tractable model system to dissect the molecular events underlying virus-induced toxicity in NPCs.
source: While a detailed mechanism for virus-induced toxicity in NPCs remains elusive, rAAV, with its exceedingly simple genome, broad tropism, and inability to replicate, offers a tractable model system to dissect the molecular events underlying this important phenomenon.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential utility of rAAV as a model system.

claim: The DG is involved in hippocampus-dependent behavioral pattern separation and pattern completion.
source: Both theoretical and experimental studies indicate that the DG is involved in hippocampus-dependent behavioral pattern separation and pattern completion (Chawla et al., 2005; Deng et al., 2013; Lacy et al., 2011; Leutgeb et al., 2007; McClelland et al., 1995; Treves and Rolls, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental studies.

claim: DG activity and computations appear to depend on the addition of abDGCs.
source: Moreover, DG activity and computations appear to depend on the addition of abDGCs (Clelland et al., 2009; Ikrar et al., 2013; Sahay et al., 2011), whose net effect is to quiet activity in mature DGCs and the rest of the hippocampus (Berdugo-Vega et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on the role of abDGCs.

claim: The net effect of abDGCs is to quiet activity in mature DGCs and the rest of the hippocampus.
source: Moreover, DG activity and computations appear to depend on the addition of abDGCs (Clelland et al., 2009; Ikrar et al., 2013; Sahay et al., 2011), whose net effect is to quiet activity in mature DGCs and the rest of the hippocampus (Berdugo-Vega et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Inhibition on mature DGCs through monosynaptic or polysynaptic inhibition is thought to enhance pattern separation by selectively suppressing competing engrams.
source: This inhibition on mature DGCs through either monosynaptic (Luna et al., 2019) or polysynaptic inhibition (Jinde et al., 2013; Toni et al., 2008) is thought to enhance pattern separation by selectively suppressing competing engrams (Espinoza et al., 2018; Johnston et al., 2016; McAvoy et al., 2016; Sahay et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on mechanisms of pattern separation.

claim: rAAV-induced ablation of neurogenesis results in a dose-dependent increase in mature DGC activity 4 weeks after infection.
source: Consistent with this idea, rAAV-induced ablation of neurogenesis results in a dose-dependent increase in mature DGC activity 4 weeks after infection, as measured by immediate early gene expression (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The retrograde labeling of DGCs by injecting AAV retro into CA3 provides an important advance for future studies of the DG.
source: The retrograde labeling of DGCs by injecting AAV retro into CA3 provides an important advance for future studies of the DG, as DGCs can now be imaged and manipulated using genetic tools while leaving adult neurogenesis intact (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 demonstrating preserved neurogenesis with functional imaging.

claim: More than 100 clinical trials using AAV vectors have claimed vector safety.
source: More than 100 clinical trials using AAV vectors have claimed vector safety (Choudhury et al., 2017; Hocquemiller et al., 2016; Hudry and Vandenberghe, 2019), resulting in two FDA-approved therapies for treating genetic diseases of the CNS (Hoy, 2019; Smalley, 2017; Mendell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews of clinical trials and FDA approvals.

claim: High rates of AAV infection exist among humans.
source: Despite high rates of infection among humans (Thwaite et al., 2015), AAV infection has not been associated with illness or pathology (Büning and Schmidt, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on AAV seroprevalence.

claim: AAV infection has not been associated with illness or pathology.
source: Despite high rates of infection among humans (Thwaite et al., 2015), AAV infection has not been associated with illness or pathology (Büning and Schmidt, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous review.

claim: Intravenous administration of rAAVs at clinically relevant titers is less likely to cross the blood-brain barrier and reach the SGZ of the DG with sufficient MOI to ablate neurogenesis.
source: Given the steep dose response of rAAV-induced cell death measured in our study, intravenous administration of rAAVs at clinically relevant titers is less likely to cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and reach the SGZ of the DG with sufficient MOI to ablate neurogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the dose-response data and knowledge of BBB permeability.

claim: High MOI may reach the SGZ in clinical trials where rAAV is injected intrathecally or directly into brain tissue.
source: Also, high MOI may reach the SGZ in clinical trials where rAAV is injected intrathecally (U.S. National Library of Medicine, 2017) or directly into brain tissue (Castle et al., 2018; Tuszynski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge of delivery routes and supported by citations to clinical trials.

claim: The extent of ablation induced by rAAV is striking and shows no signs of recovery throughout the duration of the experiments.
source: While attenuation of neurogenesis may occur in patients undergoing other treatments such as chemotherapy (Hodge et al., 2008) or radiation treatment (Saxe et al., 2007), the extent of ablation induced by rAAV is striking and shows no signs of recovery throughout the duration of our experiments.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing persistent loss at 3 months and citations to other treatments affecting neurogenesis.
